This should remove the delay for subsequent completion requests, the delay would still be there for the initial request. I think we could improve on this by using the [textDocument/didOpen](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#textDocument_didOpen) and [textDocument/didClose](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#textDocument_didClose) signals to manage the cache. This way Godot could start loading the owner, when the script gets opened. Depending on the time between opening and typing something (which can be quite a bit in bigger projects from my experience) this might completely remove the delay or decrease it a bit.

Also Godot resource loading system has a builtin cache which would definitely come in handy with the preloading approach. As long as the loaded resource isn't freed it will be reused in the future. We could just cache the references to the loaded scene and re instantiate it since this shouldn't cause much overhead (this would also allow replacing `SceneCache` with a normal `HashMap`).

This could work kinda like this:
- in `didOpen`:
    - use `ResourceLoader.load_threaded_request` to start loading the owner
    - add an invalid `Ref` to the hashmap for the path (we need to keep track of this in case the user opens files but does never complete anything)
- in `completion`:
    - use `ResourceLoader.load_threaded_request` again to make sure a loading process is going on for completions after the first one
    - obtain the resource with `ResourceLoader.load_threaded_get` (blocking like before if the resource isn't fully loaded yet)
    - then safe the resource into the hash map under the path (this will keep the resource in memory thus automatically using the resource loader cache in the future)
- in `didClose` (and on disconnect for external editor crashes):
    - remove entry from hash map and if entry was invalid use `ResourceLoader.load_threaded_get` to prevent leaking results

Hey thanks,

the SceneCache is only a wrapper for a HashMap with a Scene specific clear() function. 

Also as these Scenes are loaded resources and their sub resources also, the ResourceLoader already uses the cache for all of them, if there are used in another loaded Scene.

For the rest, sounds reasonable. I'll look into it. Also I have really fast completion times even at the beginning now with a production build and large resources (~1GB loaded), as the main slowdown came from the queue of loading->freeing->loading->freeing.

Ah k. I used a production build (ucrt). On my dev build it was in deed still very slow, even for the first input. But I did not stop time, so could just be my imagination over being happy that it worked. 🙃
That said, I think, its a good idea to load the scene when opening the script.

I moved all logic for the Scene loading into its own class SceneCache inside language_server_protocol.

Threaded resource Loading is added and used, when "use thread" is activated for the language server.
Its quite nice, as the loading now does not block the server for auto completion etc. And as far as I can see, the Scene is only used for Node path completion - definitively a win on scenes with large resources.

Using threaded resource loading is a bit of a hassle, as there is no option to kill a specific running task. (Or at least I did not found one.) So the server needs to wait for a running task and clean it afterwards, if the client disconnects or closes the document.
Also running multiple tasks in parallel that might load the same sub resources can bring up errors in the editor, so I opted for one task at a time.

But for now, I think it works quite well.

Hey, thank you very much for reviewing. :)

Ah ok, I did not look to deep into the usage of the scene itself for auto completion. I get were you are coming from, but I think it is the better user experience to instantly get an auto completion from the language server after opening a script.
Completion suggestions change in both cases. If you wait it changes basically every time from only editor suggestions to editor suggestion + ls. If you do not wait it only changes for the specific completions. 
I think the coolest thing, about the threaded resource load is, that it does not block any other language server operations.

Yes, I didn't describe my problem correctly. What I'm talking about is the following part of the spec:

> [Note that a server’s ability to fulfill requests is independent of whether a text document is open or closed.](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#textDocument_didOpen)

So yes clients must implement those notifications, but they are not required to actually open the file before performing other requests. (They do in practice so it's a good optimization to make, but completely relying on this behavior kinda goes against the spec from my understanding)

From the Specs:

> The document change notification is sent from the client to the server to signal changes to a text document. Before a client can change a text document it must claim ownership of its content using the [textDocument/didOpen](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#textDocument_didOpen) notification. In 2.0 the shape of the params has changed to include proper version numbers.
> 
> Before requesting information from the server (e.g., [textDocument/completion](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#textDocument_completion) or [textDocument/signatureHelp](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#textDocument_signatureHelp)), the client must ensure that the document’s state is synchronized with the server to guarantee reliable results.

As I understand it, the Client must claim the document with `didOpen` and can not expect reliable results from `completion` without doing so and even needs sending a `didChange` beforehand.
So the question stands from the beginning. Should a completion request be delayed until the requested document path is cached. From a UX side I still think no, but I understand how this is the expected behavior from a technical side.
So I ll add: When the cache for a path is requested, it will finish loading first. 
With the caching started as soon as a document opens, it is still well optimized as you stated.

Well from how I understand it, if a client did not claim ownership of a file with `didOpen` it is synced by definition, because the state on disc has to be the current state in the client as well. But that's very unlikely to happen for completion.

I still think it's worth to account for it. Because while such a scenario would not be realistic for completion, it might be for other requests (e.g. symbol lookup) which could happen in some sort of "read only" mode. This way we keep the option to introduce owner based behavior in such endpoints. (If we don't account for it, we need to document clearly in which scenarios the owner cache can be used.)

> Sorry for the delay, to be honest I'm having a hard time wrapping my head around this code. Like I can review the inner method code, and it looks mostly good aside from some minor stuff. But the control flow is really complicated to me, and I haven't really had the concentration to give it a full review.
> 

I made the structure more clear (hopefully).
1. I moved the script_queue and current load handling incl. the owner into a small struct. This keeps the state of the loading, script_queue and owner very clean as it correctly handles the state itself.
2. I did a little bit of renaming so it should be more clear what everything does.
3. I let the poll function handle the calling based on state and removed the inner function calls from these functions. This should make the flow way more clear.
4. I added some more fail guards like a check weither the FS is even ready. Even though I never ran into any error in the last month using this on a medium sized project. 

> However I suspect the current approach is not ready for big projects. Instances are cached based on script paths, not their own path. That means for big projects were a scene could contain a lot of scripts, this implementation would not reuse the instance between scripts. This might have quite a negative effect on memory usage.
> 
> I don't have a realistic project to verify this assumption, but I think we need to cache based on owner path, and cache the loaded owner for a given script separately to prevent this potential issue.

I am not with you on this one. Feels like a grand over-optimization. Instances are afaik cheap and resources are shared. Instancing an already loaded scene happens instantly without any measurable impact on performance or memory. Even if you would instance 20 or 30 or 50 instances of the same scene. Would be pretty bad for godot, if that would heavily impact performance. But who opens 50 scripts (or even 20) in a session not even talking about a scene with 50 distinctive scripts?  
Or are we talking about different things here?

Also, now the flow is pretty clear. A scene instance is added to its corresponding script. If you close this script the instance gets freed not interfering with any other open script that might have the same owner. 

And last but not least. In my eyes everything is better than the current state, where every auto-completion request fully loads a scene. Even the first iteration of this PR without background loading would have been a huge improvement without any real drawbacks in contrast to the current state.

> * Usage of `ERR_FAIL_COND` at top of functions to make clear in what state the function is expected to be called. E.g. `_cache_current_requested_resource` has an early return is the queue is empty. This makes it hard for me to tell the context in which the method can be called. Realistically it does only make sense to call this method when the queue is not empty, so this should be an explicit error. `ERR_FAIL_COND(resource_request_queue.is_empty())`.

Thats cool. I did not now about this convention. 

Thanks for reviewing. :)
